conditions.method: Python ast; SLOC excludes blank lines, comments and docstrings; branch points = if/for/while/try/except/with/match/boolean-op/conditional-expression/comprehension nodes

findings: ReAct is the smallest loop (57 SLOC, 12 branch points); plan-and-execute is 47 SLOC; the verified graph is 139 SLOC plus a 86-SLOC graph engine it depends on.
Supervisor-worker is 136 SLOC with 36 branch points; peer handoff is 107 SLOC with 22.
Journal replay adds 60 SLOC and wraps any loop unchanged; snapshot checkpointing needs a hook inside each loop instead.
limitations: Size of a reference implementation, not of a production system: no async I/O, streaming, auth or schema migration.
Shared infrastructure (runtime, tracer, simulator) is excluded from every row.
complexity.question: How much code and branching does each pattern cost to own?
complexity.title: Implementation complexity

findings: Restart-from-scratch completes 35% of crashed runs correctly; every failure is a duplicated notification (0.96 duplicates per run) and it re-issues 7.0 model calls on average.
Snapshots and the journal both stop at 88% / 88% without idempotency keys: the failures are exactly the crashes that land between a non-idempotent effect and its record.
Adding idempotency keys closes that window for every strategy that persists progress: snapshot+idem 100%, graph_checkpoint+idem 100%, journal+idem 100%.
Recovery cost in re-issued model calls: journal 0.00, snapshot 1.00, graph checkpoint 0.00, restart 7.00.
Bytes written to the durable store per run: journal 9374, per-iteration snapshot 48963, per-node graph checkpoint 240621 (snapshots rewrite the whole growing state each time).
limitations: Crashes are injected only around tool calls, not inside model calls or store writes; torn writes are delegated to SQLite transactions.
The backend honours idempotency keys perfectly and forever. Real APIs expire keys and some offer none.
The journal relies on the agent code being deterministic; that holds here by construction and must be enforced in real code.
durability.question: After a process crash at any point, which persistence strategy finishes the task without repeating side effects, and at what cost?
durability.title: Durable execution and crash recovery

findings: With a perfect model and no surprises all loops succeed; plan-and-execute uses 2 model calls and 995 tokens per task versus 16 calls and 7405 tokens for ReAct (-87% tokens).
Two relocated keys cost ReAct 2 extra model calls and plan-and-execute 2 replans; plan-and-execute tokens rise +199% but stay below ReAct.
At an 8% slip rate (half silent) ReAct and plan-and-execute succeed on 56% and 56% of tasks - identical, because neither can see a silent error. The verified graph reaches 95% for 5183 tokens.
On 29-step tasks the gap widens: 31% (ReAct) vs 80% (verified graph). ReAct's peak context is 1254 tokens and its total is 25244.
Auditing after every step instead of only before side effects changes success from 95% to 96% and model calls from 7.8 to 15.8.
limitations: The simulated model never mis-plans structurally; real planners also omit or mis-order steps, which favours interleaved loops more than shown here.
Slip probability is independent per attempt and identical across loops (paired draws). Real models make correlated errors.
The verifier is modelled as an independent check with a fixed miss rate; a verifier that shares the actor's blind spots would catch less.
loops.question: How do interleaved, plan-first and verified loops trade model calls, tokens and correctness?
loops.title: Execution loops

findings: Full history grows quadratically: 7347 tokens at 15 steps, 82950 at 57 (peak context 2271).
A 6-message window succeeds on 0% / 0% / 0% of tasks: it livelocks, re-fetching one evicted operand while the other falls out of the window (60 tool calls until the iteration cap vs 15 needed).
A window large enough to finish is not automatically cheaper: at 57 steps window-16 uses -4% tokens vs full history and window-32 +23%, because re-fetching adds model calls.
A 16-message window succeeds on 100% / 100% / 100%; a 32-message window on 100% / 100% / 100%, using 97.0 tool calls at 57 steps (vs 57.0 needed).
Compaction keeps 57-step tasks at 100% success with -33% tokens vs full history, paying 3.0 extra (summarisation) model calls.
The fact ledger is cheapest: -51% tokens at 57 steps, peak context 777, no extra model calls.
limitations: The simulated summariser is lossless for task facts. Real summaries drop or distort details; treat the compaction numbers as an upper bound.
The simulated model has no recall degradation with context length ('context rot'), so full history is never penalised for size, only charged for it.
The ledger needs structured tool outputs keyed by step; free-text observations require a model call to extract facts.
memory.question: How should an agent bound its context as a task grows, and what breaks when it forgets?
memory.title: Context and memory management

findings: On 57-step decomposable tasks the supervisor uses 11093 tokens vs 82852 for one ReAct agent (-87%): each worker starts from a fresh context (peak 446 vs 2269 tokens).
Peer handoff is the most expensive: 165774 tokens (2.0x the single agent), because the full transcript travels with every one of 25 handoffs and each handoff is an extra model call.
Parallel workers cut wall-clock: makespan 23.0s with 3 workers per skill vs 39.6s with 1 and 48.1s single-agent, for the same total tokens.
The supervisor makes more model calls than the single agent (85 vs 58): coordination adds calls even while it removes tokens.

Agent crash: the supervisor reassigns and finishes 50% correctly (the rest duplicate a notification), 100% with idempotency keys. A plain handoff chain finishes 0%; with a durable baton and a replica 50%, and 100% with keys.
limitations: Tasks decompose cleanly and the decomposition is always correct. A published taxonomy (MAST, arXiv:2503.13657) lists 14 failure modes observed in real multi-agent systems; this simulator models exactly one failure class, an agent crash.

Workers return compact structured facts. Open-ended research tasks return long prose and can use far more tokens than a single agent (Anthropic reports about 15x chat usage for its multi-agent research system).
Parallelism is a virtual-time schedule computed from measured per-subtask durations, not real concurrent execution.
orchestration.question: When does splitting work across agents pay off, and which topology survives an agent crash?

conditions.attack: a looked-up record carries text instructing the agent to send data to an outside recipient

findings: With no policy, and with a tool-name allowlist, the injected `send` to `attacker` executes in 100% and 100% of runs: the attack uses a tool the task legitimately needs.
An attentive reviewer blocks all of them (0% exfiltration) at 2.0 approval requests per task; a reviewer who approves everything blocks none (100%).
An argument-scoped capability token blocks all of them (0%) with zero human requests, and task success stays at 100%.
limitations: This validates enforcement mechanisms, not attack resistance: the injection is a fixed marker and the model's susceptibility is a parameter.
The capability policy works because the legitimate recipient set is known in advance. Open-ended recipients need a different control (data-flow tracking such as CaMeL, arXiv:2503.18813).
Reviewer attentiveness is binary here. Real approval fatigue is gradual and grows with request volume.
permissions.question: Which enforcement point stops an injected instruction from causing an unauthorised side effect?
permissions.title: Authorization and approval

conditions.retry: max 4 attempts, 100ms base, 2s cap, full jitter

findings: Transient faults: everything completes, but model-mediated retry spends 20.3 model calls per task versus 16.5 with runtime backoff (11247 vs 7710 tokens).
Sustained outage: backoff alone makes 62 backend calls and takes 72s; breaker + replica fallback makes 27 and takes 26s (2.7x faster).
Ambiguous timeouts on a non-idempotent tool: without idempotency keys every stack succeeds on only 54% of tasks (duplicate sends); with keys 100% and 100%.
limitations: Fault processes are independent per call; real outages are correlated across tools and time.
The replica always holds fresh data. A stale replica would turn the fallback into a silent-error source.
Simulated time: latencies and timeouts are fixed constants, not distributions.
recovery.question: Should the model, the runtime, or a circuit breaker handle tool failures - and when is a retry unsafe?
recovery.title: Failure handling and retries

conditions.cost_unit: abstract units per 1k tokens (12x price ratio)

findings: ReAct: all-large succeeds 88% at cost 30.4; all-small 44% at 2.8. The cascade reaches only 48%: it escalates on loud errors but silent errors give it no signal.
Verified graph: the cascade reaches 98% at cost 17.1 versus all-large 100% at 20.7 (-18% cost).

Keeping the verifier on the small model too ('cascade, small verifier') costs 7.4 and reaches 94%: most of the routed cost is the strong verifier re-reading the transcript, and most of the reliability comes from it.
Role routing on the verified graph: 100% at cost 18.5. On ReAct it equals all-small because every ReAct call has the same role.

Configurations above 90% success, cheapest first: verified_graph/cascade, small verifier (94%, 7.4); verified_graph/cascade (escalate on failure) (98%, 17.1); verified_graph/role (plan/verify large) (100%, 18.5).
limitations: Prices and error rates are assumptions chosen for a 12x price ratio; they are not measurements of any real model.
The large model's slips are a strict subset of the small model's (coupled draws). Real models fail on different inputs.
No learned router is evaluated; RouteLLM-style routers need preference data this simulator cannot provide.
routing.question: Can a router buy large-model reliability at small-model prices, and what does it need to work?
routing.title: Model selection and cost

findings: Exposing all 40 schemas on every call costs 33440 prompt tokens per task; scoping to the task's three capability domains costs 7008 (-79%); lazy discovery costs 9433 (-72%).
Lazy discovery pays 3 extra model calls per task (one search per capability) and ends with 5 schemas loaded.
With 10% malformed calls, the static registry lets 1.81 bad calls per task reach the backend; schema validation in the scoped registry stops 1.70 per task before execution and 0.11 reach the backend.
limitations: The simulated model never picks a wrong tool, so the accuracy cost of a crowded tool list (reported in RAG-MCP, arXiv:2505.03275) is not reproduced; only the token cost is measured.
Search is keyword matching over 40 tools. Retrieval quality at thousands of tools is a separate problem.
Prompt caching, which discounts repeated tool schemas on real APIs, is not modelled.
tools.question: What does it cost to show the model every tool, and what do scoping and lazy loading buy?
tools.title: Tool registries and capability routing

conditions.replay: ReplayModel + ReplayTools serve recorded results; request fingerprints must match

findings: A flat event log costs 17420 bytes per ReAct run (36 events); the derived span tree is 10958 bytes (35 spans).
Replay from the recorded tape reproduced the complete event stream (payloads and timestamps) exactly in 100% of runs at worst, across all three loops, with zero backend calls.
The trace is dominated by model-call payloads; plan-and-execute traces are smallest because they contain the fewest model calls (14984 bytes vs 17420).
limitations: Events store full model responses but only a fingerprint of each request; reconstructing prompts requires replaying.
Span timing uses the simulated clock.
tracing.question: What does it cost to record a run, and can a recorded run be replayed exactly?
tracing.title: Tracing and replay
